core.p: Compare how prejudice is presented in **Half-Caste** and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. In your answer, you should consider the poets’ use of language, form and structure, and the influence of the contexts in which the poems were written. (20 marks)

bullets: Similarity: first-person voices, Caribbean English, rhetorical confrontation, humour, ending with the speaker in control.
Difference: Agard’s logical, extended irony and free verse vs Zephaniah’s rhythmic, rhyming dub style and refrain; a label vs institutional stereotyping (school).
core.p: Hinge: **humour as resistance**. Both Caribbean-heritage performance poets confront British racism through humour and dialect, but they aim at different targets: Agard at a single word, Zephaniah at a system of stereotypes.
Where you see **[add a short quotation]**, insert 2–5 words from your anthology copy. In the exam, Half-Caste would be printed, so you could quote it directly; No Problem must come from memory.

plan: Targets: a word vs a system
Humour: logic trap vs relaxed confidence
Language and form: free verse/Creole vs dub rhythm/refrain
essays.q: Compare how prejudice is presented in Half-Caste and one other poem.
essays.t: Model essay: Half-Caste and No Problem
essays.text:
Agard and Zephaniah both turn prejudice back on the prejudiced, using humour and Caribbean English as weapons; however, Agard dismantles a single racist label through sustained ironic logic, whereas Zephaniah exposes a whole system of stereotyping and refuses to let it define him.

The target of each poem shapes its method. Agard’s speaker focuses on one word, and the poem begins with an exaggerated apology for being ‘half-caste’ [add a short quotation from the opening], delivered while standing on one leg. The mock politeness is ironic: by taking ‘half’ literally, the speaker exposes the absurd assumption that a mixed-race person is incomplete. Zephaniah’s target is broader. His speaker describes how others, especially at school, steered him towards sport rather than recognising his academic ability [add a short quotation about sport or school], so the prejudice is not one insult but a pattern of expectations built into institutions. Both poems therefore show prejudice as something done to the speaker by others, but Agard locates it in language itself, while Zephaniah locates it in society’s structures.

Both poets use humour, but in different ways. Agard’s humour is a logical trap. He asks whether Picasso, mixing red and green, made a ‘half-caste’ painting; whether the English weather, mixing light and shadow, is half-caste; and whether Tchaikovsky, mixing black and white keys, wrote a half-caste symphony. This tricolon of rhetorical questions draws on art, nature and music, much of it from the listener’s own celebrated culture, so the listener cannot answer without exposing their own illogic. Zephaniah’s humour is lighter and more assured: his title phrase, a relaxed everyday expression, is ironic because the poem is about a serious problem, and the speaker repeatedly insists that the problem is not him [add the title refrain]. Agard wins the argument; Zephaniah declines to take the prejudice seriously enough to argue at all.

Form and language make identity visible. Agard writes in free verse with no punctuation and lower-case letters, moving from Standard English into phonetic Caribbean Creole; the rejection of written ‘rules’ mirrors the speaker’s rejection of labels, and his command of both varieties shows that he is anything but ‘half’. Zephaniah also writes phonetically, in a Jamaican-influenced voice, but his two-stanza structure and strong, regular rhythm reflect dub poetry and reggae, the music of his heritage. His first stanza sets out the stereotyping; the second answers it with confidence. Both forms are designed to be performed aloud, which matters: these are voices that refuse to be silenced or ‘corrected’ into Standard English.

The endings show each poet’s response to prejudice. Agard’s speaker invites the listener to come back with the whole of their eye, ear and mind [add a short quotation from the ending], and only then will he tell them the other half of his story; the conflict could be resolved, but the responsibility to change lies with the prejudiced person. Zephaniah ends with a joke and a changed refrain that widens his personal experience to Black people in Britain more generally, so the poem ends in collective pride. These choices reflect the poets’ contexts: Agard, who moved from Guyana to Britain in 1977, writes about a casual term used by white Britons; Zephaniah, who grew up in Birmingham, left school at 13 and experienced racism from teachers and police, writes about stereotypes he lived through. Ultimately, both poets present prejudice as the real deficiency: Agard by showing that the listener only half-listens, Zephaniah by insisting that the problem belongs to those who label him.
essays.thesis: Agard and Zephaniah both turn prejudice back on the prejudiced, using humour and Caribbean English as weapons; but Agard dismantles a single racist label through sustained ironic logic, while Zephaniah exposes a whole system of stereotypes and refuses to let it define him.
why: **AO2**: irony, tricolon of rhetorical questions, free verse, punctuation, phonetic spelling, two-stanza structure, refrain, endings.
**Comparison**: humour as resistance, sustained in every paragraph.
**AO3**: Guyana and migration; Birmingham, dyslexia, school stereotyping, linked to targets and tone.
**Copyright-safe**: paraphrased throughout; insert your own short quotations at the marked points.
